/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.headline: Father of Noah, three, thanks those who searched for his son as village reels from loss
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.excerpt: The father of Noah, the three-year-old boy who was found dead after going missing from a playground, has spoken of his heartbreak and thanked the community who launched a tireless search for his son. Rhys Woods said there were “no words to describe the pain of this loss”, adding that the family was “absolutely heartbroken”. The small village of Brantham, in Suffolk, had mobilised on Tuesday, when Noah went missing after becoming separated from a relative at 2.37pm. He is thought to have gone down a woodland path towards the pond where his body was found. More than 1,300 people from the village and beyond descended on the area to search for Noah. They scoured the woodlands and fields around the area close to the River Stour on the Essex border as helicopters flew overhead. On Wednesday afternoon, a body was discovered at the pond, a short walk from the playground. Woods said: “Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much. It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation. “The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives.” On Thursday, the normally busy playground from which Noah disappeared was silent, save for the crying of people leaving bunches of flowers, which lined the length of the wooden fence surrounding the park.
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.trail: Rhys Woods says there are ‘no words’ for his family’s pain after Noah’s body was found in pond near Suffolk playground

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.headline: Body found in search for three-year-old Noah Woods
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.excerpt: Police searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing from a playground on the Suffolk-Essex border have found a body. Noah Woods was last seen at 3pm on Tuesday in Merriam Close, Brantham, near Manningtree, before becoming separated from a relative. The body was found in Decoy Pond in the village. In a statement, Supt Tom Pearse, from Suffolk constabulary, said: “Police and fire teams this afternoon sadly recovered the body of a child from Decoy Pond in Brantham. “Formal identification has yet to take place, but the family of Noah Woods have been informed of this development. The discovery of the body is currently being treated as not suspicious, but unexplained. “The coroner will be informed of this development. Since Noah was reported as missing, officers have carried out multiple inquiries, including the deployment of special search officers and dog units, and received support from various agencies, including helicopters from the National Police Air Service and HM Coastguard. “Additional assistance on the ground has been provided by HM Coastguard, Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service, Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue and over 1,300 members of the public supporting the search. “First and foremost, our thoughts are with Noah’s family and all those who know them. Since Noah was reported missing, vast numbers of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah, and the support for his family.

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.headline: Suffolk police release footage of Noah Woods as search for missing boy continues
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.excerpt: A massive search operation is under way in and around a Suffolk village for a missing three-year-old boy with autism, supported by hundreds of volunteers. Suffolk police have said the hunt for Noah Woods remains a missing persons investigation with no indication anything sinister has happened. Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and partially deaf, went missing after a visit to a play area in the village of Brantham on Tuesday afternoon when he became separated from a relative. Police have said Noah will not respond to his name if called. In an update on Wednesday, Supt Tom Pearse from Suffolk police said: “This is being treated as a missing person investigation at this stage and there is nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place although we keep an open mind as to the circumstances.” The force released new CCTV stills and footage of the little boy in the play area in Merriam Close just before he vanished. It is thought that he ran down an alleyway beside the playground towards a nearby new-build housing estate. The surrounding area includes woods and a pond and is near the River Stour and a railway. Noah is white with curly ginger hair and was wearing a white T-shirt featuring the TV character Bluey, shorts, and black Vans trainers with a white stripe. On Wednesday, volunteers could be seen in hi-vis jackets helping to search the area, with efforts being coordinated from the village hall and a leisure centre.
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.trail: Hundreds of volunteers join hunt for three-year-old who went missing on Tuesday afternoon

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.headline: ‘These are human fires, not wildfires’: Dunwich reflects on the devastation
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.excerpt: A local community pulling together, emergency services saving homes and caravan parks from catastrophe, and farmers and nature reserve wardens working to rapidly create fire breaks to halt a marauding fireball 40 metres high – there was plenty to praise the week after a swathe of east Suffolk burned. But local people were also in tears at the blackened, ruined state of more than 112 hectares (277 acres) of Dunwich Heath, mourning the devastation of a much-loved nature reserve alongside neighbouring Minsmere. The rare birds that inhabit the reserve have lost crucial habitat, while the rare invertebrate species there will have been “decimated”, according to the reserve staff. The fire started on Wednesday 29 July; the cause is still unknown, but Suffolk Fire Service said the fire took hold at a “ferocious pace” owing to the hot weather, dry conditions and changing winds. More than 100 firefighters have attended the scene since then, and crews from 18 fire services were in attendance. A week later, the above-ground fire has been subdued. The fire service has measured temperatures below ground exceeding 600C and surface temperatures of 60C. Hot winds and a lack of rain leave the dry, sandy region in a state of high alert for further outbreaks, with many evacuated residents advised not to return home. Locals and visitors have been kept away from an area of Dunwich Heath because the fire exposed unexploded ordnance from the second world war.

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/noah-woods-died-lea.excerpt: Hundreds of people have been evacuated and a major incident declared after a wildfire spread over more than 80 hectares (200 acres) on the coast of Suffolk, just a few miles from the Sizewell B nuclear power station. The fire – which had been described by one witness as “apocalyptic” – was said to be stabilising on Thursday night. The statement was posted by Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service, which said at least 12 fire crews were remaining overnight in the area. Jon Lacey, the chief fire officer at Suffolk fire and rescue, said earlier in the evening: “The wind change has helped a little bit, unexpectedly, and also a helicopter [dropping water] is helping to dampen the fire down.” The wildfire came a day after half of England was declared to be officially in drought, including East Anglia and six other areas. On Thursday, Natural Resources Wales declared a drought across the whole of Wales, which is on course for its driest July since records began nearly 200 years ago. As the climate crisis supercharges “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather, the UK and Europe are seeing back-to-back heatwaves that encourage vegetation to grow but then dry it out, producing ideal fuel for fires. Firefighters have responded to 393 wildfires across England and Wales in July, making it the busiest month on record and placing significant pressure on crews and resources. Phil Garrigan, the chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council, said: “Wildfires are no longer isolated or seasonal events.

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.headline: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas charged over alleged dinghy slashing in Channel
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.excerpt: The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage and failing to disclose his phone pin to police following an incident in the Channel on Tuesday, where he allegedly slashed a dinghy while a French rescuer was on board. Thomas, 37, of no fixed abode, has been charged with one count of criminal damage along with an offence under section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (Ripa), for allegedly failing to comply with a notice to disclose a phone pin to police. He has been remanded in custody to appear via videolink at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday. The charge came as the Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year. Responding to the figures, the government said it would “push further and harder” to crack down on the people organising the crossings. Chris Derrick, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “The CPS has decided to prosecute Daniel Thomas following an investigation by Hampshire constabulary into an incident on Tuesday 22 September. “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.headline: Reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways rise by fifth in a year
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.excerpt: The number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways has risen by a fifth to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year. Unions said the “horrendous” figures showed the need for more staff and policing, as the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) revealed a sharp increase in assaults on the travelling public and on railway staff last year. There were 13,464 reported assaults against passengers and members of the public on the mainline railway in 2025-26, up 36% on the previous year and the highest number recorded by the ORR since it started tracking the figures in 2004. Assaults on rail staff were up 12% in a year to 11,289 reported incidents, mainly verbal abuse but including nearly 2,500 physical assaults – an average of about seven every day. The assaults on members of the public included startling rises in cases of harassment, up 52% year on year, and common assault, up by 30%. The figures partly reflect increased reporting and zero-tolerance campaigns on public transport, but also underline concerns flagged by unions about the threats to frontline workers as well as passengers, and the availability of transport police. The RMT general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said the numbers were horrendous but chimed with the union’s own surveys showing two-thirds of its members had experienced some form of violence at work in the past year. He said: “We are calling for a significant increase in staffing across public transport, including an end to lone working.
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.trail: Unions say record high of nearly 25,000, including assaults on rail workers and public, shows need for more staff and policing

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.headline: Firms fined £1.3m after man killed by window that fell from luxury property in London
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.excerpt: Two companies have been fined a total of £1.3m over health and safety breaches after a coach driver was killed by a falling window pane. Mick Ferris, 53, was crushed when a window fell 26 storeys from the Corniche, a luxury development in Vauxhall, London, on 2 October 2018. The property developer St James Group Ltd was fined £1m and the specialist facade contractor Lindner Prater was fined £300,000 at a sentencing hearing at Inner London crown court on Thursday. The firms were also ordered to pay costs of £125,000 each. In August, the firms were found guilty of ignoring “foreseeable risks” and convicted of “failing to discharge a duty” under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. Ferris, who was a driver for Clarkes of London, had been returning to his coach when the window pane, which weighed 130kg and was roughly 85cm wide and 190cm tall, fell from a height of about 90 metres (300ft). During the trial, the court heard that a window panel had previously fallen from the same development in August 2017, but that the design had not subsequently significantly changed. The Corniche, located on Albert Embankment alongside the Thames, has panoramic views over the Houses of Parliament. Luxury flats in the building – containing a gym, pool and spa – have been listed for sale at £3m. Ferris’s widow, Rachel, said his death “could have happened to anybody” and could have been prevented.
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.trail: Mick Ferris was crushed to death when the 130kg pane fell 26 storeys from the Corniche housing development

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.headline: ‘Cash to trash’ levy on house developers too low to offset damage to Norfolk Broads, say critics
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.excerpt: A new levy on developers to allow almost 16,000 homes to be built in the environmentally protected Norfolk Broads has been cut by tens of thousands of pounds per house, the Guardian can reveal. Ministers say the government’s environmental delivery plans (EDPs) were created to unblock housing growth across the country and are a “win-win” for development and nature. They allow environmental damage to protected habitats and species to be overlooked as long as developers pay into a nature restoration fund, which is used for conservation actions at a later date designed to address the impacts. Once the first instalment of the fee is paid, work can start immediately. Labelled by critics as “cash to trash”, the first EDP was published last week by the government’s nature adviser, Natural England. It allows 15,780 houses to be built within the Norfolk Broads, a heavily protected wetland network of 60 shallow lakes and winding rivers that is home to some of England’s rarest species. The published plan, which is open for consultation for 28 days, states that the developer will pay £2,675 per house – £42m in total – into the nature restoration fund to cover compensatory actions including fenland creation and restoration, a change in use of agricultural land to semi-natural habitat, catch-dyke restoration and deer management. But a previous draft of the EDP, seen by the Guardian, set the levy much higher.
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/daniel-thomas-court.trail: Exclusive: Levy that allows almost 16,000 houses to be built on Norfolk Broads will not cover cost of mitigating environmental damage, critics say

/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.headline: UK defence contractors to offer 40,000 apprenticeships, placements and jobs
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.excerpt: Defence contractors have promised to create 40,000 apprenticeships, work experience placements and jobs for young people each year, as Wes Streeting claimed to be overseeing a “ministry for growth”. Labour is keen to demonstrate that the rapid increase in defence spending planned for the coming years, which may necessitate tax rises, will result in jobs in the UK. In particular, Streeting said he was determined the defence industry should play its part in tackling what he called the “moral emergency” of almost 1 million 16-to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet). “I think we have a responsibility, as we’re investing more in the defence of the realm, to do so in a way that boosts British jobs, British industry, and helps to deal with this moral emergency,” he said. “I want the Ministry of Defence to be a ministry of growth and a ministry of opportunity, and that’s how we’re going to direct our defence spending.” The defence secretary was speaking before a roundtable with leaders from large contractors, including BAE Systems, MDBA and Rolls-Royce. The firms have signed up to a series of pledges aimed at opening up more opportunities for young people. They have promised to offer 40,000 18- to 24-year-olds each year an opportunity in the sector by 2030 – whether via work experience, an apprenticeship or a permanent role. That is scheduled to rise to 50,000 by 2035.
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.trail: Wes Streeting says he leads a ‘ministry for growth’ as Labour seeks to show more defence spending will create UK jobs

/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.headline: ‘The chancellor is in a bind’: is No 11 at odds with Burnham’s big vision?
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.excerpt: Until now, Andy Burnham has been a lucky prime minister. In office for just over six weeks, no major domestic crisis derailed his plans over the summer, Reform has been on the back foot, and he arrived back at Westminster with his personal approval ratings soaring and optimism undampened. But underneath the sense of relief that many Labour MPs are feeling that their high-stakes gamble of ousting Keir Starmer appears – for now – to have paid off, there is an unease that Burnham’s premiership is yet to make contact with economic reality. In their early weeks in office, his team were able to point to some inherited green shoots: below-forecast inflation figures, sustained growth, signs that sluggish productivity could be starting to turn around. All despite the economic turmoil unleashed by the Iran conflict. This week, all that changed. With the end of summer recess came a global bond sell-off amid anxiety over oil prices, sticky inflation and pressure to ramp up defence spending, which pushed government borrowing costs to their highest since the 2008 financial crash. It makes the backdrop to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a difficult one. Economists reckon about half of the £24bn fiscal breathing space his predecessor Rachel Reeves had built up at her spring forecast has since been wiped out by higher inflation and interest rates, severely limiting Healey’s room for manoeuvre.
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.trail: MPs applaud PM’s ambition and optimism but John Healey has yet to show he can match leader’s radical perspective

/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.headline: John Healey warns of tough first budget as Middle East war puts pressure on economy
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.excerpt: The chancellor has indicated that the UK will face a tough budget next month due to Trump’s war in the Middle East. In an interview with the Financial Times, John Healey said the conflict in Iran would probably have a strong influence on his first budget on 28 October. Healey, who succeeded Rachel Reeves when Andy Burnham became prime minister in July, told the newspaper he wanted to ensure the country had a robust “buffer against uncertainty” amid increasing global instability. However, economists have predicted that Healey will need to raise taxes or implement significant cost-cutting measures to protect the £24bn fiscal headroom that Reeves had after her March statement. “What’s happening in the Middle East is hitting inflation, it’s hitting growth, it’s hitting borrowing costs,” Healey said. “It’s part of a more dangerous world that is more uncertain and it’s one of the challenges we have to meet in this country, but have to meet with other [countries].” Healey declined to say how much headroom he aimed to have, but insisted he and Burnham were “in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules”. The newspaper said he planned to stick to Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledges not to raise taxes on “working people”, such as income tax, national insurance contributions or VAT, and was also not expected to raise the rate of corporation tax. The public finances are under pressure from soaring global bond yields , which hit an 18-year high earlier this week.
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.trail: Chancellor says he wants to ensure country has ‘buffer’ against uncertainty as global bond yields hit 18-year high

/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.headline: Burnham tries to calm bond market fears as sell-off threatens crucial first budget
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.excerpt: Andy Burnham moved to calm volatile bond markets on Wednesday as surging borrowing costs threatened to wreck plans for his government’s crucial first budget next month. After a days-long sell-off of government bonds – and with the chancellor, John Healey, facing the prospect of sharply reduced spending power, Burnham used his first appearance at prime minister’s questions to promise decisions would be “grounded in fiscal responsibility”. That was widely seen as an attempt to soothe investors after his statement to parliament on Tuesday, in which he made bold promises of more public control of utilities, further interventions on the cost of living and a recommitment to a 3% increase in defence spending. While those offers were broadly welcomed by Labour MPs, Burnham was criticised by others for inflaming the sell-off. His former economic adviser, Jim O’Neill, said it was the “last thing” the markets needed. Investors across world markets have been dumping government bonds amid fears about rising inflation, runaway deficits and competing demand for capital from tech companies on a debt-fuelled AI spending spree. The sell-off has driven up yields, or interest rates, including in the UK. At one point on Wednesday, the cost of 10-year borrowing for the government hit its highest level since 2008, at 5.29%, before easing slightly. That is expected to be costly for Healey when the Office for Budget Responsibility draws up its budget forecasts.
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.trail: Prime minister promises his government will make decisions ‘grounded in fiscal responsibility’

/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.headline: Fund defence spending from tax rise on middle earners, thinktank tells Healey
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.excerpt: The chancellor, John Healey, must be prepared to raise taxes for middle earners if he wants to fund significantly higher defence spending, the Resolution Foundation thinktank has said. Healey resigned from Keir Starmer’s government in June, protesting against what he argued was the then prime minister’s failure to adequately fund defence. But in his new post in No 11 Downing Street, Healey has made clear that he will wait until next year’s spending review before presenting a plan to meet Labour’s pledge of devoting 3.5% of GDP to defence by 2035. In a new report, entitled Thin End of the Wedge, economists at the Resolution Foundation suggest he will not be able to raise the £28bn a year it would take to meet that promise without asking average workers to pay more. They say that despite historically large tax rises since Labour came to power in 2024, amounting to £70bn a year, the “tax wedge” – taxes on earnings, minus benefits – remains low by international standards. “Despite recent increases, the UK still taxes average earners less than most of our international peers,” says the foundation’s chief economist, James Smith. The analysis shows that tax rises under Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, resulted in a 2.4 percentage point jump in the tax wedge last year – the largest for any country in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
/politics/2026/sep/25/labour-appoints-ma.trail: Resolution Foundation argues that UK’s internationally low ‘tax wedge’ must rise to pay for defence ambitions

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/jeffrey-donaldson-s.headline: Drumcree ruling raises fears of sectarian confrontation in Northern Ireland
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/jeffrey-donaldson-s.excerpt: The boiling cauldron known as Drumcree that used to scald and torment Northern Ireland each summer gradually cooled two decades ago, leaving it as a name for the history books. Instead of pitched battles between Orangemen and police around the parish church near Portadown in County Armagh, and the murderous sectarian violence they triggered across the region, gave way to a de facto truce. The Orange Order still wished to march down Garvaghy Road in the run-up to 12 July celebrations – a route opposed by the mainly Catholic residents – but its members no longer tried to storm lines of police who dug trenches and erected barbed wire to stop them. Fury dwindled after 1998, when the mayhem threatened the nascent Good Friday agreement, and the Orangemen settled for annual peaceful, ritualised protests. However, a court ruling this week ignited a political row over Drumcree and raised the spectre of renewed confrontation next July. On Tuesday, the high court in Belfast quashed the latest in a series of determinations that have prevented the march from proceeding down Garvaghy Road since 1998. The commission accepted that its decision-making process had been flawed. Billy Gamble, one of six commissioners, resigned. Unionist parties hailed the ruling as an overdue comeuppance for a statutory body that adjudicates on contentious marches.
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/jeffrey-donaldson-s.trail: High court quashes latest restriction on Orange Order march, reigniting political row over Garvaghy Road

/uk-news/2026/sep/25/jeffrey-donaldson-s.headline: Current and ex-DUP members knew of allegations about Jeffrey Donaldson, party says
/uk-news/2026/sep/25/jeffrey-donaldson-s.excerpt: Former and current members of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) knew of allegations about the former leader Jeffrey Donaldson but did not share them, the party has said. Information about Donaldson was not reported through “appropriate channels” and left the party unable to formally respond, the DUP leader, Gavin Robinson, said on Monday. The admission came as new claims about Donaldson’s conduct engulfed the party in crisis a week after he was convicted of sexual abuse against children in a case that shocked Northern Ireland. It is alleged that the former Lagan Valley MP sexually pestered women, visited a gay sauna while denouncing homosexuality and got drunk on foreign trips – and vomited over the mayor of Beijing – while professing to be a teetotaller. The claims came after a jury at Newry crown court on 22 June unanimously found the 63-year-old guilty of 18 sexual offences, including one count of rape, against two women when they were children. He is to be sentenced in September. The Belfast Telegraph reported that he is expected to appeal. The DUP joined other parties in welcoming the verdict and stressed that it had suspended Donaldson when he was first charged in 2024. However its hopes of containing the political damage have dissolved amid a clamour over what the party knew – and when – about other misconduct by Donaldson.

/music/2026/sep/25/woman-who-accused-jay.headline: Jay-Z 30 tour review – the sheer profusion of nailed-on classics is dizzying
/music/2026/sep/25/woman-who-accused-jay.excerpt: Jay-Z’s first solo tour in nine years bills itself as a celebration: it marks the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt. But it feels less concerned with nostalgic reverie than a show of strength in the present day. Hip-hop is a genre predicated on constant forward motion, in which careers tend to burn brightly, then dim as the music moves on. Jay-Z may not be the only fiftysomething rapper out on a career retrospective tour in 2026, but he is, unequivocally, the only one who’s capable of doing it at this level: packing out the biggest stadiums in the world nearly a decade after he last released an album, his standing impressively undiminished by a retreat into semi-retirement. Moreover, he’s doing it in considerable style. The show’s musical approach can clearly trace its origins back to 2001, the year Jay-Z solved the problem of how on earth a rapper was supposed to appear on MTV Unplugged by eschewing hip-hop’s standard DJ-and-backing-tapes approach and employing a live band: the Roots were apparently astonished to be asked, but the end result was pretty jaw-dropping. Back in May, his first solo gig in five years essentially recreated it – he headlined the Roots’ annual Picnic festival with Questlove and co in tow once more – but the Jay-Z 30 tour supersizes it, featuring not just a 10-piece band, but an 18-piece string section.
